title: Stonewall Gap Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Stonewall Gap wells have a 60-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs estimated at $8,100-$15,300.
intro_html:
If you are buying land or planning a home near Stonewall Gap, the local permit record gives a useful starting point. Wells within 5 miles have a median reported depth of 60 feet, and the middle half runs from 45 to 140 feet. Reported yields are also generally workable, but the record is incomplete: 213 wells report depth, 77 report pump yield, and 22 report static water level.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and nearly all named aquifers are listed as unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. That makes neighboring-well research important before you price a new well or commit to a lot.

sections.heading: Stonewall Gap well depths vary across the plains
sections.html:
The local median well depth is 60 feet. Half of the wells with reported depths fall between 45 and 140 feet, so a driller working on a typical Stonewall Gap parcel may be pricing a relatively shallow hole. The depth distribution is not uniform, however: 67% are under 100 feet, 20% are 100-300 feet, 8% are 300-600 feet, and 5% reach 600 feet or more.

The deepest recorded well is 1,110 feet. That outlier matters when comparing bids. Alluvium and plains sedimentary rock can produce very different drilling conditions from one parcel to the next, and permits identify 400 wells with unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Use the 60-foot median as a planning point, not a guarantee.

sections.heading: Most Stonewall Gap wells report useful production
sections.html:
Among the 77 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 7.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute, which is a solid range for many household uses when the well, pressure system, storage, and permitted use are properly designed.

Production is not uniformly strong. The records show 71% in the 5-15 gallon-per-minute range, 17% at 15 or more, 10% between 1 and 5, and 1% under 1 gallon per minute. A buyer should ask for the actual well construction report and pumping information, not rely only on the area median. A low-yield well may still work with storage, but it deserves a different budget and operating plan.

sections.heading: The recorded water level is shallow, but the trend is unclear
sections.html:
Only 22 wells in the Stonewall Gap data report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth sample. Within that group, the median depth to water is 20 feet, and the middle half is 11-39 feet. Those figures suggest that water is often encountered relatively close to the surface in the reported wells.

The permit history does not provide a water-level series by decade, so it does not establish that the water table is rising or falling. Static water level can also differ by location, season, pumping history, and well construction. Have a driller check nearby logs and measure the well being considered before relying on a shallow-water assumption.

sections.heading: Permit activity runs from the 1950s through 2025
sections.html:
Stonewall Gap has a long permit history, with 408 wells in Colorado Division of Water Resources records and 245 recorded as constructed. Permit activity was highest in the 2010s, with 101 permits, followed by 98 in the 1990s and 60 in the 2000s. The newest permit in the supplied record is from 2025.

The most active named drillers are Boday Well Drilling, also recorded as Boday, Alex, with 47 wells; Snyder Well Pump Service, also recorded as Snyder, Marion M., with 37; and Authorized, recorded as Pe, Pg, with 32. These records show local experience, but they are not a recommendation or a guarantee of availability. Confirm licensing, scope, references, and what each bid includes.

sections.heading: A Stonewall Gap well may cost more than the hole itself
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 60-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $2,100-$3,300. This is only the drilling portion and should not be treated as the complete project price.

A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,100-$15,300 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing or grout requirements, water treatment, or a low-yield design can change the bid. Ask every driller to separate drilling, casing, development, testing, pump equipment, trenching, and electrical work.

sections.heading: Check water quality, yield, septic, and building limits
sections.html:
Environmental screening deserves attention before buying. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 354 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 17 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These mapped sites do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to order a water test and investigate the parcel's history, drainage, and nearby land uses.

Low yield and dry-hole risk still need a site-specific review, especially because most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Confirm the well permit and allowed use with Colorado DWR. Check septic setbacks, soil conditions, access for a rig, trench routes, building location, and the distance between the well and septic system. A parcel that can support a well may still need a different house or septic layout.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Stonewall Gap, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Stonewall Gap is 60 feet. The middle half runs from 45 to 140 feet. About 67% of reported wells are under 100 feet, but the deepest record reaches 1,110 feet. Use nearby well logs rather than the median alone when estimating a new well.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Stonewall Gap?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,100-$3,300. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,100-$15,300. Access, depth, casing, water treatment, and low yield can move the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Stonewall Gap wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 77 wells with reported pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 7.0-14.0. Most reported wells, 71%, produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Results vary by parcel, so obtain the well log and pumping information before assuming a new well will match the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Stonewall Gap?
faq.a: The permit map shows 354 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with 17 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those mapped locations do not determine the quality of one private well. Test the well for appropriate contaminants, review nearby land uses, and retest after construction or equipment changes.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a Stonewall Gap lot with a well?
faq.a: A well permit and a recorded well do not by themselves confirm that a lot can support your planned home. Check the permitted use with Colorado DWR, then verify water quality, yield, septic suitability, setbacks, access, and electrical or trench routes. Most local permits are domestic or household use, but the proposed project must match the permit.
